sub.en: Each linker says something different about the order of events.

items.q: ___ the balloon was high in the sky, they said their son was inside it.
items.why: as soon as = immediately after. One event follows the other with no gap.

items.q: ___ the balloon landed, the story was already on television.
items.why: by the time = before that moment. It is normally used with the past perfect or already.

items.q: Nobody checked the story ___ a week later.
items.why: until = up to that point and not before.

items.q: ___ reporters were interviewing the family, the boy said too much.
items.why: while introduces a longer action, so it takes the past continuous.

items.q: ___ the police arrived, the crowd had already gone.
He kept quiet ___ his brother told the newspapers.
___ she heard the news, she phoned her sister.
It turned ___ that the photograph had been made on a computer.
items.why: it turned out that = we discovered later that.

rows: When the boy spoke, the reporters stopped.
While they were filming, he said too much.
As soon as it landed, the news went out.
By the time they arrived, it had ended.

lines: [As soon as|Until|By the time] the photograph appeared online, thousands of people shared it.
[While|As soon as|Until] the newspaper was checking the story, the picture [was circulating|circulated once|had circulated] everywhere.
[By the time|While|As soon as] the editor called, the story [had already gone|already went|has already gone] out.
Nobody said anything [until|by the time|as soon as] a reader wrote in.
[When|While|Until] they finally checked it, it [turned|was turning|had turned] out to be a hoax.

items.why: by the time normally takes the past perfect in the other clause.
as soon as marks a short, complete event, so the past simple is used.
until means not before that point; by the time means already finished before it.

acts.title: Too good to be true
text: Every good hoax has the same shape. Somebody creates a story that people want to believe, and by the time anybody checks it, half the world has already read it.

Take the balloon story. A couple in the United States let a large gas balloon float away, and as soon as it was high in the sky they announced that their six-year-old son was inside it. The police were informed and helicopters were sent up to track it. By the time the balloon landed, about eighty kilometres away, the story was live on television. When the boy was not found inside, reporters concluded that he had fallen out during the flight. In fact he had been hiding at home the whole time. The parents kept quiet until, while reporters were interviewing the family on air, the boy mentioned that they had done it to get on television.

Older hoaxes worked the same way, only more slowly. In 1912 two men announced that they had found a jaw and a skull that proved the link between early humans and apes. Most scientists accepted the conclusion until, nearly forty years later, tests showed that the bones were a fake. By then the man most people consider responsible had died, and science had wasted four decades on a lie.

Interestingly, the internet has not invented anything new. What has changed is speed. A photograph can now circulate for three days consecutively before a single person asks where it came from. Surprisingly, the newest hoaxes are often the smallest: a fruit that does not exist, a phone trick that does not work. Personally, I find those the hardest to argue with. Nobody expects a lie to be that boring.

items.s: The parents announced that their son was in the balloon only after it was high in the sky.
The boy was found inside the balloon when it landed.
The boy himself said on television why the family had done it.

The text says the internet has invented a completely new kind of hoax.
According to the writer, the newest hoaxes are often small ones.

write.q: Write the story of a time you believed something that was not true — a rumour, a news story, a message from a friend. Use as soon as, by the time and until at least once each, and finish with It turned out that… or In the end…
write.model: A few years ago a message circulated saying our university was closing for a week. As soon as I read it, I forwarded it to about thirty people. By the time I got to my first class, half the group had already made plans to travel home. Nobody checked it until one student phoned the office. It turned out that somebody had invented the whole thing as a joke. In the end nothing happened, but I have never forwarded a message that quickly again.
